title: Choosing the best answer
goal: Five steps, the same every time: read the question, find the proof, check each answer, cross out the traps, answer.

card.title: READ → FIND → CHECK → ELIMINATE → ANSWER
lines: READ the question twice. Say the job. Watch for NOT, EXCEPT, BEST and how many answers it wants.
FIND the proof in the passage before you look at the answers.
CHECK each answer against the proof.
ELIMINATE: cross out the wrong ones and name the trap.
The four traps: THE OPPOSITE · NOT THERE · TRUE, BUT NOT WHAT THEY ASKED · HALF RIGHT.

N.label: not there
N.feedback: It may sound sensible, but it is not in the passage.

T.label: true, but not what they asked
T.feedback: It is in the passage, but it answers a different question.

H.label: half right
H.feedback: Part of it is right and part of it is wrong, or it goes too far.

popcorn.title: The Snack Counter
sentences: Movie theatres make surprisingly little money from tickets.
For a big new film, a large share of each ticket price goes back to the studio that made the movie, especially in the first weeks after release.
The theatre keeps more as the weeks go by, but by then most people have already seen the film.
This is why the snack counter matters so much.
Popcorn costs a theatre only cents to make, yet a large bag can sell for eight dollars or more.
The same is true of fountain drinks.
The money from snacks stays with the theatre, and it pays for staff, cleaning, and the giant screens and sound systems that customers expect.
Some theatres have tried lowering snack prices to attract more visitors, but most found that people bought the same amount either way.
Theatre owners also know that the smell of popcorn in the lobby is itself a kind of advertising.
Many theatres pop fresh batches on purpose during the busiest times, even when they already have plenty ready.

yawn.title: Why We Yawn
sentences: Most people think a yawn means you are tired or bored, but scientists are not sure that is the whole story.
Yawning happens more often when the brain is warm, and a deep yawn pulls in cool air and stretches the jaw, which may help cool the brain down.
This could explain why people yawn more in warm rooms than in cold ones.
Yawning is also catching: seeing, hearing or even reading about a yawn can start one.
Researchers think this "contagious" yawning may be linked to empathy, since people tend to catch yawns more easily from friends and family than from strangers.

geese.title: Why Geese Fly in a V
sentences: Every fall, Canada geese cross the sky in a shape like the letter V.
The shape is not for show.
Each goose flies slightly behind and to the side of the one ahead, where the moving air gives it a small lift.
This means most of the flock uses less energy than a bird flying alone.
The goose at the front gets no help, so it has the hardest job.
When the leader gets tired, it drops back and another goose takes its place.
The V has a second advantage: every bird can see the others, which helps the flock stay together.
Geese also honk while they fly.
Scientists think the honking helps the birds keep track of one another, especially in fog or at night.
Together, these habits let a flock travel hundreds of kilometres in a single day.

salt.title: Salt on Winter Roads
sentences: When snow is coming, trucks spread salt on Canadian roads.
Salt does not melt ice by being warm.
It works because salty water freezes at a lower temperature than plain water, so a thin layer of salt keeps ice from sticking to the pavement.
Salt has limits, though.
Below about minus ten degrees Celsius it works slowly, and in extreme cold it hardly works at all.
On those days, many cities spread sand instead, which does not melt anything but gives tires something to grip.
Salt also causes damage.
It rusts cars and bridges, and when the snow melts it washes into streams and lakes, where it can harm fish and plants.
For this reason, some cities now mix their salt with beet juice, which helps it stick to the road so that less is needed.
Even so, plain salt is still the most common choice because it is cheap and it works on most winter days.

sections.title: Five steps
sections.tutorNote: I DO. Read the five steps and the four traps. Reveal the worked example one step at a time, thinking aloud; the point of FIND is to hold the proof before meeting the answers. Then match each trap to what it means. On screen the answers stay covered until the proof is tapped, and the traps are named after the answer is chosen.

text: Most test questions give you four answers. Three of them are traps.
Use five steps, the same every time.
READ the question twice and say the job.
FIND the proof in the passage before you look at the answers.
CHECK each answer against the proof.
ELIMINATE: cross out the wrong ones and name the trap.
The traps have names. If you can name the trap, it cannot catch you.
THE OPPOSITE: the passage says the reverse.
NOT THERE: it sounds sensible, but the passage never says it.
TRUE, BUT NOT WHAT THEY ASKED: it is in the passage, but it answers a different question.
HALF RIGHT: part is right and part is wrong, or it goes too far with a word like ALWAYS or NEVER.
On screen, you answer first. Then you name the trap in each wrong answer.

steps.title: Watch one

reveals.label: READ
reveals.text: Twice. The job: a reason, about why the snack counter matters. One part.

reveals.label: FIND
reveals.text: The answers stay covered. Search words: SNACK COUNTER. Sentence 4 says 'This is why the snack counter matters so much.' THIS points back, so I read the sentences before and after it.

reveals.label: FIND: read back
reveals.text: Sentences 1 to 3: theatres keep little of the ticket money.

reveals.label: FIND: read on
reveals.text: Popcorn costs cents and sells for eight dollars. And sentence 7: 'The money from snacks stays with the theatre.' That is my proof.

reveals.label: CHECK (b)
reveals.text: 'Because snacks are cheap to make and the money stays with the theatre.' That matches my proof.

reveals.label: ELIMINATE (a)
reveals.text: 'Because customers expect popcorn.' The passage says customers expect big screens and sound, not popcorn. NOT THERE.

reveals.label: ELIMINATE (c)
reveals.text: 'Because tickets are expensive.' The passage never says tickets are expensive. It only sounds right because of what I already know. NOT THERE.

reveals.label: ELIMINATE (d)
reveals.text: 'Because the studio sells the snacks.' The passage says the snack money stays with the theatre. THE OPPOSITE.

reveals.label: ANSWER
reveals.text: (b) is what is left, and it matches the proof.
